title: Bending Light: Reflection & Refraction
summary: Bend mirrors and lenses by hand to discover how reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection actually work.
theory: Light travels in straight lines until it meets a new surface, where it obeys one of two rules. **Reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; curving the mirror (concave) gathers parallel rays to a single **principal focus (F)**, related to the radius of curvature by f = R/2. **Refraction**: light changes speed crossing between media, bending its path according to Snell's Law, n = sin i / sin r. A convex lens uses this to focus light to a point whose position depends on the object distance u relative to f (1/v − 1/u = 1/f). When light inside a denser medium hits a boundary steeper than the **critical angle** (sin θc = 1/n), it undergoes **total internal reflection** and cannot escape at all — the principle behind optical fibres.

procedure.title: Bend the concave mirror
procedure.description: Drag the glowing ring on the mirror's rim to change its curvature and watch the focal point F move.

procedure.title: Find the burning point
procedure.description: Slide the paper screen until it sits exactly at F and observe what happens; then switch to bulb mode and place the bulb at F to produce a parallel beam.

procedure.title: Squash the convex lens
procedure.description: Drag the candle and the lens, and use the bulge handle to change the lens's focal length. Note how the image changes from real & inverted to virtual & magnified as the candle crosses F.

procedure.title: Find the critical angle
procedure.description: Drag the torch inside the glass/water/diamond block and sweep the angle until the beam suddenly stops escaping — that is the critical angle, and beyond it you get total internal reflection.

procedure.title: Build an instrument
procedure.description: On the optician's bench, arrange the two lenses and the object to complete each mission: a telescope, a microscope, and a projector.

observation: The mirror's focal length shortens as its curvature deepens, matching f = R/2. The lens image flips from real/inverted to virtual/magnified exactly when the object crosses the focal point. Total internal reflection begins abruptly once the incidence angle passes the critical angle predicted by sin θc = 1/n, with denser media (diamond) showing a much smaller critical angle than water or glass.

quiz.question: Bending a concave mirror to a deeper curve (smaller radius of curvature) will:

options.text: Move the focal point farther away
Move the focal point closer to the mirror

quiz.explanation: Since f = R/2, a smaller radius of curvature R produces a shorter focal length f, pulling the focus closer to the mirror.

quiz.question: A candle placed exactly at a convex lens's focal point produces:

options.text: No image — the outgoing rays are parallel

quiz.explanation: At u = f, the lens equation gives v = infinity: every ray leaves the lens parallel to the axis, so no image forms.

quiz.question: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels:

options.text: From a denser medium into a rarer medium, above the critical angle
From a rarer medium into a denser medium, at any angle

quiz.explanation: TIR requires light moving from higher to lower refractive index, and only once the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle sin θc = 1/n.

title: Panamá Canal: Lock & Lift System
summary: Explore the physics of the Panama Canal lock system using gravity, buoyancy, and hydrostatic pressure to move ships.
theory: The Panamá Canal lock staircase uses a series of water-filled chambers and miter gates to lift ships from sea level to Gatún Lake. Gravity flow valves move water between chambers—no pumps are required. A ship's buoyancy and hydrostatic pressure equalize the water levels, allowing safe transit across the continental divide.

procedure.title: Execute Step
procedure.description: Progress through the 13-step sequence to see how water is moved to change the ship's elevation.

procedure.title: Monitor Live Readouts
procedure.description: Observe the ship elevation, chamber levels, and water moved as the gravity flow valves open.

procedure.title: Change Speed and View
procedure.description: Adjust the simulation speed and use the interactive 3D view to inspect the lock mechanism from different angles.

observation: Water flows by gravity from higher to lower elevation chambers. The ship is safely lifted by buoyancy as water fills its current lock chamber.

quiz.question: How is water moved between the locks in the Panamá Canal?
quiz.explanation: The canal relies entirely on gravity flow valves to move water between chambers.

quiz.question: What physics principle allows the ship to be lifted within the lock?
quiz.explanation: As the water level rises in the chamber, buoyancy lifts the floating ship along with the water.

title: Reverse an Array: In-Place Swap
summary: Master the Two-Pointer technique to reverse an array in-place with O(1) auxiliary space.
theory: Reversing an array or string in-place is a fundamental computer science concept. By using a Left and Right pointer and swapping elements directly, we achieve **O(1) auxiliary space** (no extra memory allocated) and **O(N) time complexity** (linear time).

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Drop two markers on the track: L at the first block, R at the last block.

procedure.title: Swap in Place
procedure.description: Swap the block at L with the block at R without allocating a new array.

procedure.title: Move Markers Inward
procedure.description: Slide marker L one step right and marker R one step left, until they meet or cross.

observation: For an 11-letter word, only 5 swaps are needed! Using two pointers is extremely memory efficient compared to creating a duplicate string.

quiz.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of reversing a string in-place using two pointers?
quiz.explanation: We only need memory for two variables (L and R) regardless of the string's length, meaning it requires O(1) constant auxiliary space.

title: Reverse a String: Out-of-Place
summary: Understand why reversing immutable strings requires O(N) extra memory space.
theory: In many programming languages, strings are **immutable**, meaning their characters cannot be modified in-place. To reverse a string without converting it to an array, we must create a completely new string in memory and build it character by character from the end of the original string. This approach results in **O(N) auxiliary space** because we allocate new memory proportional to the string's length.

procedure.title: Allocate New String
procedure.description: Observe how a brand new empty string must be created in memory.

procedure.title: Iterate Backwards
procedure.description: Watch a pointer start at the end of the original string and move backwards.

procedure.title: Concatenate
procedure.description: See each character get appended to the new string, allocating more memory space each time.

observation: Reversing an 11-letter string this way allocates 11 new character slots in memory. Compare this to the Array version, which required 0 extra slots!

quiz.question: Why does reversing an immutable string require O(N) auxiliary space?

options.text: Because it takes N operations to reverse.
Because you must create a new string of length N in memory.
Because strings take up more memory than arrays.
It doesn't, it takes O(1) space.

quiz.explanation: Since the original string cannot be modified, a new string of size N must be built, consuming O(N) extra memory.

title: Palindrome Checker: Two-Pointer Convergence
summary: Use two converging pointers to verify if a string is a palindrome in O(N) time and O(1) space.
theory: A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards (e.g., 'racecar'). The most efficient way to check for a palindrome is using the Two-Pointer technique. We place a pointer at the start (L) and end (R) of the string. We compare the characters at these pointers. If they match, we move the pointers inward. If they don't match, it is not a palindrome. We repeat this until the pointers meet in the middle.

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Place L at the first character and R at the last character.

procedure.title: Compare Characters
procedure.description: Check if the character at L is identical to the character at R.

procedure.title: Converge
procedure.description: If they match, move L right by 1 and R left by 1. Stop if they don't match.

observation: Notice how the pointers act as a mirror, checking symmetry from the outside in.

quiz.question: What happens the moment the characters at L and R do NOT match?

options.text: The loop continues until they meet.
The function immediately returns False (it is not a palindrome).
The pointers jump back to the start.

quiz.explanation: A single mismatch proves the word is not perfectly symmetrical, so we can stop checking immediately.

procedure.title: Launch the Coaster
procedure.description: Release the coaster and watch the trade between kinetic and potential energy.

title: ESP32 Prototype Bench
summary: Wire an ESP32 DevKit on an interactive 3D breadboard, check pin constraints, monitor serial output, and generate Arduino sketches.
theory: The **ESP32** is a versatile micro-controller with integrated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. When prototyping with microcontrollers, understanding GPIO pin constraints is essential: some pins are **input-only** (GPIO 34-39), some are **strapping pins** that affect bootloader mode (GPIO 0, 2, 12, 15), and others conflict with the Wi-Fi ADC2 subsystem. The prototype bench lets you wire circuits with jumpers, check pin assignments against hardware rules, and inspect the generated Arduino firmware in real time.

procedure.title: Select a Bench Preset
procedure.description: Choose between presets like Weather Station, Parking Sensor, or Hover-Vehicle Bottle, or start with an Empty Bench.

procedure.title: Add Parts from the Bin
procedure.description: Pick sensors, LEDs, displays, or actuators from the parts bin to drop them onto the workbench mat.

procedure.title: Wire Jumpers in 3D
procedure.description: Click pins on the ESP32 and components to connect jumper wires. Rotate and zoom the 3D view or switch to Top View for precision.

procedure.title: Verify Pin Rules & Checks
procedure.description: Open the Checks tab to ensure no strapping pin conflicts, power rail shorts, or ADC2 Wi-Fi clashes exist.

procedure.title: Run Simulation & Inspect Sketch
procedure.description: Click Run to power the board, observe the live circuit and Serial Monitor at 115200 baud, and copy the auto-generated Arduino sketch.

observation: Safe microcontroller wiring prevents boot failures caused by strapping pin pull-ups and avoids ADC2 channel conflicts when Wi-Fi is active. The generated sketch dynamically reflects your GPIO connections.

quiz.question: Which of the following ESP32 GPIO pins can only be used as inputs?
quiz.explanation: GPIs 34, 35, 36, and 39 do not have internal pull-up or pull-down resistors and cannot be configured as digital outputs.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid using ADC2 pins when Wi-Fi is enabled on the ESP32?

options.text: They draw too much power from the 3.3V rail
The ADC2 hardware is shared with the Wi-Fi driver and causes read errors when Wi-Fi is active
They invert the serial monitor baud rate

quiz.explanation: The ESP32 Wi-Fi driver uses ADC2 internally; attempting to read analog values on ADC2 pins while Wi-Fi is on will fail or return invalid data.

title: Potentiometer: Internal Resistance of a Cell
summary: Balance a cell against a potentiometer wire with and without a shunt resistance, then work out the cell's internal resistance from the two balance lengths.
theory: A **potentiometer** is a long wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current from a driver cell. Because the wire is uniform, the potential difference across any length l is proportional to l, so the wire has a constant **potential gradient k** (volts per cm). A test cell is connected through a galvanometer to a sliding **jockey**; at the **null point** the galvanometer shows zero deflection, no current flows through the test cell, and the cell's voltage equals k l. **Open circuit (K₂ open):** the balance length l₁ measures the emf, E = k l₁. **Closed circuit (K₂ closed, resistance R across the cell):** a current I = E/(R + r) flows, so the terminal voltage drops to V = E − I r = k l₂. Dividing the two equations gives V/E = l₂/l₁ = R/(R + r), and therefore the internal resistance is **r = R (l₁ − l₂) / l₂**. Plotting (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is r. The driver cell's emf must be greater than the test cell's emf, and the positive terminals of both cells must be joined to the same end of the wire.

procedure.title: Check the driver circuit
procedure.description: Leave the rheostat near 2 Ω and read the potential drop across the wire. It must be larger than the cell's emf; if the status bar warns about this, reduce the rheostat resistance.

procedure.title: Find l₁ with K₂ open
procedure.description: Drag the jockey along the wire (use the slider and ±0.1 cm buttons for fine control) until the galvanometer needle sits at zero, then press Record l₁.

procedure.title: Choose a resistance and close K₂
procedure.description: Pick a resistance R from the box (for example 5 Ω) and close key K₂ so that R is connected across the cell.

procedure.title: Find l₂
procedure.description: Slide the jockey to the new null point. It will be shorter than l₁ because the terminal voltage is lower. Press Record l₂.

procedure.title: Repeat for other resistances
procedure.description: Record l₂ for at least four values of R, such as 2, 5, 10 and 20 Ω. Do not change the rheostat, or the potential gradient changes and your readings are cleared.

procedure.title: Calculate r
procedure.description: For each row the table gives (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ and r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂. Take the mean of the r values.

procedure.title: Plot the graph and check
procedure.description: Study the graph of (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R; its slope is r. Press Check my answer to compare with the cell's actual internal resistance, or try a new unknown cell.

observation: With K₂ open the balance length l₁ is the longest, since it corresponds to the full emf. With K₂ closed the balance length l₂ is always shorter, and it increases towards l₁ as R is made larger because less current is drawn and less voltage is lost across r. The values of r calculated for different R agree closely, and the graph of (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to r.

quiz.question: The working principle of a potentiometer is that, for a wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current, the potential difference across any length of the wire is:

options.text: Proportional to the square of the length

quiz.explanation: V = I ρ l / A, and with I and A constant the potential difference is directly proportional to the length l.

quiz.question: At the null point the galvanometer shows zero deflection. This means:

options.text: The driver cell has no emf
The jockey is at end A
No current flows through the test cell, so the potentiometer reads its emf

quiz.explanation: At balance the voltage along the wire exactly equals the cell's voltage, so no current is drawn. That is why a potentiometer measures emf accurately where a voltmeter cannot.

quiz.question: With key K₂ closed and a resistance R across the cell, the balance length l₂ compared with l₁ is:
quiz.explanation: When current flows, part of the emf is lost across the internal resistance. The terminal voltage V = E − I r is less than E, so l₂ < l₁.

quiz.question: The internal resistance of the cell is given by:
quiz.explanation: From E = k l₁ and V = k l₂ we get l₂/l₁ = R/(R + r). Rearranging gives r = R (l₁ − l₂)/l₂.

quiz.question: If a larger resistance R is connected across the cell, the balance length l₂ will:
quiz.explanation: A larger R draws less current, so less voltage is lost across r. The terminal voltage approaches E, and l₂ approaches l₁, but it can never exceed it.

quiz.question: No balance point can be found anywhere on the wire. The most likely reason is:

options.text: The potential drop across the wire is less than the emf of the test cell

quiz.explanation: A null point exists only if the voltage across the whole wire exceeds the cell's voltage. Reduce the rheostat resistance, or use a driver cell of higher emf.

quiz.question: Why are the positive terminals of the driver cell and the test cell joined to the same end of the wire?

options.text: To increase the current in the wire
So that the two emfs oppose each other and a null point can be found
To make the potential gradient smaller

quiz.explanation: If the cells were connected the other way round, their emfs would add and the galvanometer could never be brought to zero.

quiz.question: How can the sensitivity of a potentiometer be increased?

options.text: Decrease the potential gradient, using a larger rheostat resistance or a longer wire

quiz.explanation: A smaller potential gradient means a given error in balance length corresponds to a smaller error in voltage, so the measurement is more precise. The wire's total drop must still exceed the cell's emf.

title: Potentiometer: Comparing the EMFs of Two Cells
summary: Balance two cells in turn on a potentiometer wire using a two-way key, and find the ratio of their emfs from the two balance lengths.
theory: A **potentiometer** is a long wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current from a driver cell, so the potential difference across any length l of the wire is proportional to l. The wire therefore has a constant **potential gradient k** (volts per cm). A test cell is joined, through a galvanometer, to a sliding **jockey**; at the **null point** the galvanometer shows zero deflection, no current flows through the cell, and its emf equals the potential drop along the balance length. With a **two-way key** the two cells are connected one at a time: for cell E₁ the balance length is l₁, so E₁ = k l₁, and for cell E₂ the balance length is l₂, so E₂ = k l₂. Dividing the equations gives **E₁ / E₂ = l₁ / l₂**, because the gradient k cancels. Changing the rheostat changes k, and therefore both lengths, but not their ratio, so the experiment is repeated for several rheostat settings and the mean ratio is taken. Plotting l₁ against l₂ gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is E₁/E₂. The driver cell's emf must be greater than the emf of either test cell, and the positive terminals of all cells must be joined to the same end of the wire.

procedure.title: Check the driver circuit
procedure.description: Start with the rheostat near 2 Ω and read the potential drop across the wire. It must be larger than the emf of either cell; if the status bar warns about this, reduce the rheostat resistance.

procedure.title: Find l₁ with E₁ connected
procedure.description: Set the two-way key to E₁. Drag the jockey along the wire (use the slider and ±0.1 cm buttons for fine control) until the galvanometer needle sits at zero, then press Record l₁.

procedure.title: Find l₂ with E₂ connected
procedure.description: Without changing the rheostat, switch the two-way key to E₂, find its null point and press Record l₂. The table row for this rheostat setting is now complete.

procedure.title: Read the ratio
procedure.description: The table shows E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ for the completed set.

procedure.title: Repeat for other rheostat settings
procedure.description: Change the rheostat (for example 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 Ω) and repeat steps 2 and 3, taking at least three sets. Both lengths change with the rheostat, but their ratio should stay almost constant.

procedure.title: Find the mean ratio
procedure.description: Take the mean of E₁/E₂ over all completed sets and write the result.

procedure.title: Plot the graph and check
procedure.description: Study the graph of l₁ against l₂; its slope is E₁/E₂. Press Check my answer to compare with the actual emfs, or try two new unknown cells.

observation: For every rheostat setting the balance length of the cell with the larger emf is longer than that of the other cell. Increasing the rheostat resistance lengthens both balance lengths because the potential gradient falls, but the ratio l₁/l₂ stays nearly constant. The graph of l₁ against l₂ is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals E₁/E₂, in agreement with the mean of the table values.

quiz.question: At the null point with E₁ connected, the potential drop across the balance length l₁ equals:

options.text: The emf of the driver cell

quiz.explanation: At balance no current flows through the cell, so the potential drop k l₁ along the wire exactly equals the emf E₁.

quiz.question: The ratio of the emfs of the two cells is given by:
quiz.explanation: E₁ = k l₁ and E₂ = k l₂, so dividing gives E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂. The gradient k cancels.

quiz.question: A student finds l₁ = 800 cm and l₂ = 500 cm. The ratio E₁/E₂ is:
quiz.explanation: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ = 800/500 = 1.6. Note it is a ratio of lengths, so it has no units.

quiz.question: The rheostat resistance is increased and the experiment is repeated. The balance lengths l₁ and l₂ will:

options.text: Both increase, but l₁/l₂ stays the same

quiz.explanation: More rheostat resistance means less current and a smaller potential gradient k, so longer lengths are needed to balance the same emfs. Since k cancels in l₁/l₂, the ratio is unchanged.

quiz.question: No balance point can be found for cell E₁, although one is found for E₂. The most likely reason is:

options.text: The cell E₂ has no internal resistance
The potential drop across the whole wire is smaller than the emf of E₁
The jockey is pressed too hard

quiz.explanation: A null point exists only if the voltage across the entire wire exceeds the cell's emf. E₁ is the larger emf, so reduce the rheostat resistance.

quiz.question: Why is a two-way key used in this experiment?

options.text: To connect either cell to the galvanometer circuit, one at a time, without changing the rest of the circuit
To increase the emf of the driver cell
To reduce the current in the wire
To connect both cells in series

quiz.explanation: The two-way key lets one test cell be balanced and then the other, using the same wire, jockey and galvanometer.

quiz.question: Why must the positive terminals of the driver cell and both test cells be joined to the same end of the wire?

options.text: To make E₁ equal to E₂
So that each test cell opposes the potential drop along the wire and a null point can be found

quiz.explanation: If a test cell were connected the other way round, its emf would add to the wire's potential and the galvanometer could never be brought to zero.

quiz.question: How can the sensitivity of a potentiometer be increased?

options.text: Decrease the potential gradient, using a larger rheostat resistance or a longer wire

quiz.explanation: A smaller potential gradient means a given error in balance length corresponds to a smaller error in voltage. The wire's total drop must still exceed both emfs.

title: Sonometer (3D): Frequency of a Tuning Fork
summary: Use a 3D sonometer to find the resonant lengths of known tuning forks, verify that f × L is constant at fixed tension, and then find the frequency of an unknown fork.
theory: A **sonometer** is a hollow wooden box with a wire stretched along its top between two bridges. The tension comes from weights hung over a pulley. A wire of length L, tension T and mass per unit length μ carries waves at speed **v = √(T/μ)**. When it vibrates in its fundamental mode, the length L is half a wavelength, so its natural frequency is **f = v / 2L = (1/2L)√(T/μ)**. If a tuning fork is sounded and pressed on the box, the wire is forced to vibrate at the fork's frequency. When the length is adjusted until the wire's natural frequency equals the fork's, **resonance** occurs: the wire vibrates with a large amplitude and a small **paper rider** placed on it is thrown off. For a fixed wire and tension, **f × L = v/2 is constant**, so f is proportional to 1/L and a graph of f against 1/L is a straight line through the origin with slope v/2. This allows the unknown frequency of a fork to be found from its resonant length: **f_x = (f × L) / L_x**. The resonant length is proportional to √T for a given fork. The wire must be uniform and taut, the pulley frictionless, and the bridge must be moved slowly near resonance.

procedure.title: Set the tension
procedure.description: Choose the number of slotted weights. The hanger and weights give the tension T = Mg. Keep it the same for the whole experiment, because changing it clears your readings.

procedure.title: Select a known fork
procedure.description: Pick one of the known tuning forks, for example 256 Hz, from the chips and note its frequency.

procedure.title: Strike the fork and place it on the box
procedure.description: Press the strike button. The fork is sounding and its stem is pressed on the box close to the wire. The paper rider sits at the middle of the vibrating length.

procedure.title: Slide the bridge B₂ slowly
procedure.description: Drag B₂ in the 3D view, or use the slider and the 0.1 cm buttons. Watch the rider and the vibration bar. Near resonance the rider trembles, and at resonance it is thrown off the wire.

procedure.title: Record the resonant length
procedure.description: With the rider off, read the length from the scale. The top view shows the reading mark clearly. Press Record. Repeat for the other known forks.

procedure.title: Find the unknown fork
procedure.description: Select Fork X and repeat the procedure at the same tension to find its resonant length L_x.

procedure.title: Calculate and plot
procedure.description: Find f × L for each fork and take the mean. Calculate f_x = (mean f × L) / L_x. Plot f against 1/L and use twice the slope to find the wave speed v. Press Check my answer to compare with the actual values.

observation: The resonant length is shorter for a fork of higher frequency and longer for a larger tension. For every known fork f × L is almost the same, so the graph of f against 1/L is a straight line through the origin. The unknown fork has a frequency f_x = (f × L) / L_x, found from its resonant length. With a tension of about 25 N the wave speed in the wire is about 250 m/s.

quiz.question: The fundamental frequency of a wire of vibrating length L, tension T and mass per unit length μ is:
quiz.explanation: The fundamental mode has a loop in the middle, so L is half a wavelength. With wave speed v = √(T/μ), f = v/λ = v/2L = (1/2L)√(T/μ).

quiz.question: With the tension fixed, the vibrating length of the wire is doubled. Its fundamental frequency becomes:
quiz.explanation: f is proportional to 1/L when T and μ are fixed, so doubling L halves f.

quiz.question: With the wire and tension unchanged, which quantity stays constant for forks of different frequency?
quiz.explanation: Because f = v/2L, the product f × L = v/2 is the same for every fork, as long as the tension does not change.

quiz.question: The paper rider is thrown off the wire when:

options.text: The length of the wire equals one full wavelength
The natural frequency of the wire equals the frequency of the fork
The tension in the wire becomes zero

quiz.explanation: At resonance the wire vibrates with a large amplitude, which throws off the paper rider.

quiz.question: A 256 Hz fork resonates at L = 50 cm. An unknown fork resonates at L = 40 cm under the same tension. Its frequency is:
quiz.explanation: f × L is constant, so f = 256 × 50 / 40 = 320 Hz.

quiz.question: A graph of frequency f against 1/L for a wire at fixed tension is a straight line through the origin. Its slope equals:
quiz.explanation: f = (v/2)(1/L), so the slope of f against 1/L is v/2 and the wave speed is v = 2 × slope.

quiz.question: For the same fork, the tension in the wire is made four times larger. The resonant length becomes:
quiz.explanation: L = (1/2f)√(T/μ), so L is proportional to √T. Four times the tension gives twice the length.

quiz.question: The sonometer wire is stretched over a hollow wooden box because the box:

options.text: Acts as a sounding board that makes the wire vibrate strongly
Reduces the tension in the wire
Insulates the wire from the fork

quiz.explanation: The hollow box is a sounding board. It takes up the vibrations of the fork and passes them to the wire, and it makes the sound of the vibrating wire louder.

title: Meter Bridge: Resistance and Resistivity of a Wire
summary: Balance a known resistance against an unknown wire on a metre-long bridge wire, find the unknown resistance from the null point, and calculate the resistivity of the wire.
theory: A **meter bridge** is a practical form of the **Wheatstone bridge**. A uniform wire AB of length 100 cm is stretched along a metre scale and joined to two gaps by thick copper strips. A known resistance **R** from a resistance box is placed in one gap and the unknown wire **X** in the other. A galvanometer is connected between the middle point D of the strips and a sliding **jockey** on the wire. A cell and a key send current through AB. When the jockey touches the wire at the **null point**, at a distance l from A, the galvanometer shows no deflection and the bridge is balanced. The resistance of each part of the uniform wire is proportional to its length, so **R / X = l / (100 − l)**, which gives **X = R (100 − l) / l**. The reading is repeated for several values of R and the mean of X is taken. A graph of l / (100 − l) against R is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/X. If the length L and the diameter d of the unknown wire are known, its **resistivity** is **ρ = X A / L = X π d² / 4L**. The balance point should lie near the middle of the wire, where the percentage error is smallest. The key must be kept closed only while taking a reading, so that the heating of the wire does not change its resistance.

procedure.title: Note the wire details
procedure.description: Read the length L and the diameter d of the unknown wire from the card. In the laboratory d is measured with a screw gauge at several places.

procedure.title: Choose a resistance R
procedure.description: Pick a value of R from the resistance box. Start with about 5 Ω; a value close to the unknown resistance puts the balance point near the middle of the wire.

procedure.title: Find the null point
procedure.description: Drag the jockey along the wire, then use the slider and the 0.1 cm buttons until the galvanometer needle is at zero and the ring turns green.

procedure.title: Record l
procedure.description: Press Record. The table gives l, 100 − l and X = R(100 − l)/l. If the balance point is near an end of the wire, choose a different R.

procedure.title: Repeat for other values of R
procedure.description: Take at least four readings with different R, keeping the balance points between about 30 cm and 70 cm.

procedure.title: Find the mean and the graph
procedure.description: Read the mean X from the table. Check it with the graph of l/(100 − l) against R, whose slope is 1/X.

procedure.title: Calculate the resistivity
procedure.description: Use ρ = X π d² / 4L with the mean X. Press Check my answer to compare X and ρ with the actual values and see which material the wire is made of.

observation: The balance length l increases as R is increased, because a larger R needs a longer part of the wire to balance. For every reading the value of X = R(100 − l)/l is nearly the same, and the graph of l/(100 − l) against R is a straight line through the origin. The mean X and the dimensions of the wire give its resistivity, which agrees with a standard value for materials such as constantan, manganin and nichrome.

quiz.question: In a meter bridge, R is in the left gap and the unknown X in the right gap. If the balance length from the left end is l cm, then X equals:
quiz.explanation: At balance R / X = l / (100 − l), because the resistance of each part of the uniform wire is proportional to its length. So X = R (100 − l) / l.

quiz.question: The balance point should be near the middle of the wire (about 50 cm) because then:

options.text: The percentage error in X is smallest

quiz.explanation: The error in X caused by a given error in l is smallest when l is near 50 cm. Near the ends the same reading error produces a much larger error in X.

quiz.question: A meter bridge works on the principle of the:
quiz.explanation: The two gaps and the two parts of the wire form the four arms of a Wheatstone bridge, balanced when the galvanometer shows zero.

quiz.question: With R = 6 Ω the null point is at l = 40 cm. The unknown resistance X is:
After one reading, R and X are interchanged and the reading is repeated. This is done to:

options.text: Remove the error due to the end resistances of the bridge
Increase the current in the wire

quiz.explanation: The copper strips and connections add small resistances at the ends. Interchanging R and X and taking the mean cancels this error.

quiz.question: The resistivity of the material of the unknown wire, of length L and diameter d, is:
quiz.explanation: ρ = X A / L and the area of cross-section is A = π d² / 4, so ρ = X π d² / 4L.

quiz.question: The key is kept closed only while a reading is taken because:

options.text: The current heats the wire and changes its resistance
The galvanometer would be damaged by a small current
The wire would expand and become longer

quiz.explanation: A steady current heats the wire. Its resistance then rises with temperature and the readings are no longer for the original resistance.

quiz.question: If the diameter of a wire is doubled, with the length and material unchanged, its resistance becomes:
quiz.explanation: R = ρL/A and A is proportional to d². Doubling d makes A four times larger, so R falls to one quarter.

title: Ohm's Law: V–I Graph, Series and Parallel Resistances
summary: Vary the current with a rheostat, read a voltmeter and an ammeter, find an unknown resistance from the V–I graph, and verify the laws for resistors in series and in parallel.
theory: **Ohm's law** states that, at constant temperature, the current I through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference V across its ends, so **V = I R**. The constant R is the **resistance** of the conductor, and the graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. In the experiment a cell, a key, a rheostat and an **ammeter** are connected in series with the resistor, and a **voltmeter** is connected in parallel across it. The rheostat changes the current, and for each setting V and I are read. The ratio V / I is calculated for every reading and the mean is taken, which is checked against the slope of the graph. For two resistors in **series** the same current flows through both and the total resistance is **R_s = R₁ + R₂**. For two resistors in **parallel** the same potential difference is across both, and **1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂**, so R_p = R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂), which is smaller than either resistance. The key is kept closed only while taking a reading, so that heating does not change the resistance. A real voltmeter draws a small current, so the value of V / I is very slightly smaller than the true resistance.

procedure.title: Connect R₁ alone
procedure.description: Select R₁. The circuit shows the cell, key, rheostat, ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the resistor.

procedure.title: Set the rheostat and take a reading
procedure.description: Move the rheostat to a setting and press Take reading. The ammeter and voltmeter values are entered in the table with V / I.

procedure.title: Repeat for at least five settings
procedure.description: Change the rheostat to vary the current over a wide range. Keep the current below about 2 A so that the resistor does not heat up.

procedure.title: Find R₁ from the table and the graph
procedure.description: Read the mean V / I. Check it against the slope of the V–I graph, which is a straight line through the origin.

procedure.title: Repeat for R₂
procedure.description: Select R₂ and repeat the readings to find its resistance.

procedure.title: Series and parallel
procedure.description: Select Series and then Parallel and take readings for each. Compare the measured resistance with R₁ + R₂ and with R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) in the summary table.

procedure.title: Check your answer
procedure.description: Press Check my answer to see the actual resistances and your percentage errors. Press New resistors to practise with different values.

observation: For each resistor, V / I is nearly the same for every rheostat setting, so the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin. The measured resistance of the series combination is close to R₁ + R₂ and is larger than either resistor. The measured resistance of the parallel combination is close to R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) and is smaller than either resistor.

quiz.question: For a conductor obeying Ohm's law, the graph of potential difference V against current I is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the I axis
A straight line with a negative slope

quiz.explanation: Ohm's law says V is proportional to I at constant temperature, so V–I is a straight line through the origin.

quiz.question: The slope of the V–I graph of a resistor gives its:
quiz.explanation: V = I R, so the slope of V against I is the resistance R.

quiz.question: The ammeter and the voltmeter are connected, respectively:
quiz.explanation: The ammeter must carry the whole current, so it is in series. The voltmeter measures the potential difference across the resistor, so it is in parallel with it.

quiz.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in series. The equivalent resistance is:
Two resistors of 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
The equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel is always:

options.text: Equal to the sum of the two
Equal to the mean of the two

quiz.explanation: Each branch gives the current an extra path, so the combination conducts more easily than either resistor alone.

quiz.question: The key is kept closed only while taking a reading because:

options.text: The current heats the resistor and changes its resistance

quiz.explanation: Heating raises the temperature of the resistor, so Ohm's law no longer holds with a constant R.

quiz.question: A real voltmeter has a very large but finite resistance. The measured value of V / I for a resistor is therefore:
quiz.explanation: The voltmeter takes a small current, so the ammeter reads slightly more than the current in the resistor. V / I is then slightly less than R.
